sentences.text: Australornis grew to a length of roughly 70 to 85 cm, similar in size to a pied shag, and is estimated to have weighed between 1.5 and 2 kg.
The fossil record includes right coracoid, scapula, humerus, ulna, radius fragments, and a left carpal bone.
Australornis is considered one of the oldest known flying seabirds and was the first fossil of a non-penguin seabird discovered in New Zealand from the Paleocene epoch.
Although found near the oldest known penguin fossils, Australornis lacks any morphological resemblance to penguins.
The fossil was discovered in 2009 by amateur paleontologist Leigh Love in north Canterbury, New Zealand.
As one of the oldest known flying seabirds, Australornis likely possessed adaptations for life at sea.
The genus Australornis was named by G. Mayr and R.P. Scofield in 2014, with the type species Australornis lovei also named by them in the same year.
A 2017 study classified Australornis as a stem-anseriform within the family Vegaviidae, which is the family it belongs to.
Australornis lived during the Paleocene epoch, between 60.5 and 61.6 million years ago, with the time range for the genus estimated from 61.66 to 56 million years ago.
It is debated whether the fossil evidence is sufficient to fully substantiate phylogeny, though it supports the view that Neoaves diversification began in the earliest Paleogene.
